newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Panic in S.Leone after ousted leader's broadcast.
newsitem.headline: Panic in S.Leone after ousted leader's broadcast.

text.p: Panic gripped the Sierra Leone capital Freetown on Tuesday after a clandestine broadcast by ousted president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah stoked fear of a new attack by Nigeria which is trying to reinstate him.
The city's lorry parks were crammed with people scrambling to leave for the interior after Kabbah called on troops backing coup leaders to defect to a Nigerian-led regional force.
The chaos reigning in the West African state since low-ranking officers toppled Kabbah on May 25 looked sure to worsen with fuel stocks running out, industry sources said.
Kabbah, overthrown just over a year after his election, urged the coup leaders, who are isolated internationally, to relinquish power to save Sierra Leoneans further hardship.
"Hand over now and spare yourself and the people of Sierra Leone further pains and suffering," Kabbah said in the broadcast on an FM frequency preceded by the national anthem.

"If you persist however and cause any further force to be used...then let me assure you no Western countries will grant you asylum. No African countries will harbour you," Kabbah said, addressing the coup leaders.
He then addressed an "order" to ordinary soldiers and Revolutionary United Front rebels who fought a five-year bush war against the army but then allied with the coupmakers.

"As your commander I hereby order you to report to the nearest ECOMOG base without arms in your possession and declare your loyalty. By doing so you will avoid being treated as a mutineer," said Kabbah, who has been exiled in neighbouring Guinea since his ouster.
He accused the military junta and its guerrilla allies of killing civilians, looting and destroying the country's infrastructure.

Sierra Leone's mining economy had already been brought to a virtual standstill by the war. The violence following the coup drove away Lebanese and other foreigners controlling most private businesses, which have since shut.
The military authorities described Kabbah's broadcast as illegal and a propaganda ploy by Nigeria to give the impression to Sierra Leoneans that Kabbah had been returned to power.
An official statement told Sierra Leoneans to listen to state radio, broadcasting on a separate frequency.
The junta headed by Major Johnny Paul Koroma has publicly rejected Kabbah's return to power.

"In order to guarantee lasting peace and stability, Sierra Leone needs fresh and truly democratic elections, supervised, not merely observed, by neutral experts provided by the international community," it said in a statement last week.

The statement said the election of Kabbah in 1996 was rigged by elements in the military in connivance with the national electoral commission, and that the number of votes cast for Kabbah in the south and east of Sierra Leone was in excess of the registered voters.

Nigeria had troops in Sierra Leone under a defence pact before the coup. On June 2 its gunboats shelled the capital Freetown in a show of force, triggering clashes with Sierra Leone soldiers and rebels.
Nigeria has reinforced its troops in Fretown but has at the same time joined a regional initiative to try and resolve the political impasse peacefully.
